summary.text: 新 means ‘new’ or ‘fresh’. Early forms are analyzed as an axe (斤) with 辛 as a sound element; some forms also include 木. Another proposal connects the whole graph with splitting wood, so its construction remains disputed.

formation.text: One analysis treats the graph as phonosemantic: 斤 depicts an axe in a wood-cutting scene, while 辛 is identified as the sound component. Some early forms include 木, interpreted as depicted wood, whose strokes can merge with 辛. A competing analysis sees 新 as an expansion of 𣓀, interpreted as splitting wood with a wedge. The received Shuowen account and Duan Yucai’s revision parse it differently, leaving the construction disputed.

components.text: 斤 is analyzed as an axe in the early-form interpretation; the alternative expanded-𣓀 analysis concerns the graph as a whole.
辛 is identified as a sound element in the early-form analysis. Its modern and reconstructed readings offer comparisons, but do not by themselves prove the ancient graphic analysis.

sound_limitation.text: The paleographic analysis identifies 辛 as phonetic, but the available comparisons do not independently establish the ancient sound relationship or settle the graph analysis.

sound.text: 辛 and 新 share the Modern Mandarin reading xīn; this modern match does not establish their ancient sound relationship.
Both are transcribed as sin in Middle Chinese in the supplied Baxter–Sagart comparison; this does not alone establish the ancient graphic analysis.
The supplied Baxter–Sagart comparison gives 辛 *[s]i[n] and 新 *s.tsʰi[n]; this comparison does not alone prove the graph’s phonetic analysis.

components.text: Some early forms include 木, interpreted as depicted wood. Its strokes can share a boundary with 辛, so the elements are not always graphically distinct.

history.text: Early forms vary: some include 木 beside 辛, with strokes that may merge, while Warring States forms separate the elements differently. The selected seal-script and Western Zhou bronze-script illustrations are modern redrawings of script styles, not artifact photographs or proof of a single sequence.

The received Shuowen entry glosses 新 as ‘taking wood’ and parses it with 斤 plus a phonetic element. Duan Yucai instead reads the graph as 斤 and 木 with 辛 as phonetic; paleographic analyses offer other component accounts. These are historical interpretations, not settled proof of the graph’s origin.

uncertainties.text: Proposed analyses include 斤 plus 辛, sometimes with 木; an expansion of 𣓀; and differing Shuowen and Duan Yucai parses.

One account proposes that a firewood-related word and the different word ‘new’ sounded alike or similarly, so 新 could be reused to write ‘new’. The proposed sound match remains tentative because the depicted implement’s name and pronunciation are unverified. Early inscriptions already use 新 for ‘new’; these examples neither date nor disprove the proposed borrowing.

senses.text: An oracle-bone example, 新鬯, is glossed ‘newly brewed wine’, attesting the sense ‘new’ in the Shang corpus. This early use does not establish the character’s original meaning.
‘Recent’ and ‘modern’ are current glosses; the available account does not date their development from ‘new’.
A historical gloss and graph analysis connect 新 with taking or chopping wood for fuel, but a dated standalone use of 新 meaning ‘firewood’ is not established.

developments.text: One account proposes that a firewood-related word and the different word ‘new’ sounded alike or similarly, so the graph was reused to write ‘new’. The old implement’s name and sound are unverified, and early inscriptions already use 新 for ‘new’; the proposed borrowing and its chronology therefore remain uncertain.

limitations.text: The development of ‘recent’ and ‘modern’ from ‘new’ is not dated in the available evidence.
The proposed firewood sense rests on graph analysis and a historical gloss; no dated standalone use or original pronunciation for the depicted implement is established.

overview.text: 新 means ‘new’ or ‘fresh’. One analysis sees 斤 (an axe) and 辛 as a sound element, sometimes with 木 (wood). A firewood-to-‘new’ borrowing is proposed, but the tool’s old name and sound are unverified.

components.text: 斤 depicts an axe, associated in one analysis with chopping wood.
辛 is identified as a sound element; the proposed ancient sound link remains unproven.
Some early forms include 木, interpreted as wood; its strokes may merge with 辛.

relationships.text: 斤 is identified as an axe in the proposed early-form analysis and depicts an implement within the wood-cutting interpretation.

Early-form analyses identify 辛 as a sound element. They share Mandarin xīn and Middle Chinese sin in the cited comparison; the Old Chinese comparison is less close and does not settle the graphic analysis.
In forms that include it, 木 depicts wood within the proposed wood-cutting or firewood interpretation.
